transcript:
Header: Date: 2026-03-31 | Time: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 42m
Attendees: Avery (Redwood AE), Samira (Redwood SE), Jordan (Product), Carlos (SummitPay Head of Platform), Priya (ML Eng), Ethan (Security), Maya (PM)

Summary: Quick walkthrough of Redwood's structured output / JSON mode and function/tool-calling. Demoed schema enforcement, guardrails, and Console integration. Discussed security requirements (SOC2, KMS), deployment choices (hosted vs Dedicated vs VPC), and next steps for a pilot.

Topics: Structured output (JSON mode), Function calling, Schemas & guardrails, Redwood Console walkthrough, Redwood Optimize hints (batching/quant profiles), Security (SOC2, KMS, RBAC)

Action items (in-call): see metadata.

Transcript:
[00:00] Avery Chen: Ok hi everyone, thanks for joining, we appreciate the time. I'm Avery, I'm the AE on the account, with Samira our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Carlos: Doing good, thanks. We got about 40 minutes, we wanted to see specifically how Redwood can give us deterministic JSON outputs and tie into our downstream services with function calls.
[00:16] Samira Patel: Awesome, that's exactly what we'll focus on. Quick agenda: structured output JSON mode, what schemas look like, guardrails to prevent hallucinations, then a short Console demo showing tool/function calling and a small Optimize tipset.
[00:29] Priya Reddy: Great. We're especially worried about strict field types and not leaking PII into responses. Also latency - payments is latency sensitive.
[00:38] Samira Patel: Totally. We'll show the JSON schema enforcement, plus the SDK's validation layer and built-in redwood-runner guardrail that rejects non-conforming responses.
[00:48] Jordan Lee: I'll jump in on the Console part once Samira shows the API flow.

[02:05] Samira Patel: Alright, pulling up the Console - let me share my screen. (screen noise) So here is the Structured Output tab, you can toggle JSON mode, and you can paste a JSON schema or point to a stored schema. For demo purposes I've got a tiny schema for a transaction enrichment payload: fields for transaction_id (string), amount_cents (integer), currency (string enum), merchant_category (string), risk_score (number 0-1) and flags (array of strings).
[02:35] Carlos: When you say "schema enforcement", what happens if model returns a string for amount?
[02:40] Samira Patel: Good q - the runtime validates. There are two modes: soft validation (we attempt to coerce types and surface warnings) and strict validation which will cause the response to be rejected and optionally trigger a fallback policy - e.g., reroute to a more deterministic model or call an internal validator. For pilot we usually recommend strict for production-critical fields.
[03:02] Priya Reddy: Can strict cause increased latency if it triggers fallback?
[03:05] Samira Patel: Yes potentially, but we add policies: you can do fail-fast or try-2-tries-then-fallback. Also Optimize suggests model variants and quantization to keep token cost down while preserving latency SLO.

[04:10] Avery Chen: A quick note on deployments: you can run this on Hosted API for fastest onboarding, Dedicated for predictable throughput, or Private VPC if you need egress controls or on-prem keys. For SummitPay with PCI-adjacent workloads, a VPC/private control plane with customer-managed KMS is not uncommon.
[04:33] Ethan Shaw: Speaking of KMS, do we support HSM-backed keys or only cloud KMS?
[04:36] Jordan Lee: We support cloud KMS integrations (AWS, GCP), and HSM integrations for enterprise Private installs - we can share the security integration doc.

[06:00] Samira Patel: Back to the demo - now I'll show function/tool calling. In the API payload you can attach tool definitions; here's a small tool that hits our transaction matcher service. I'll trigger the model with a prompt that asks to produce JSON conforming to the schema and, if a high-risk flag is raised, call the matcher tool with the transaction_id.
[06:24] (typing)
[06:40] Samira Patel: Ok, running it now. You'll see streaming output in the Console - and it tries to call the tool. If the schema validator rejects the payload, the runtime logs the failure and shows the attempted output with error details.
[07:01] Priya Reddy: Can we see an example of the model's JSON and the error when it doesn't match?
[07:08] Samira Patel: Sure - here's an example from earlier. (reads) Output: {"transaction_id": "tx_9a3f", "amount_cents": "1200", "currency": "USD", "merchant_category": "retail", "risk_score": 0.82, "flags": ["velocity"] } - note the amount is a string, that's caught by the validator. In strict mode we reject. In soft mode we coerce to integer and surfacing a warning.
[07:45] Carlos: Ok that flows. What about guardrails to stop hallucinated merchant names or PII?
[07:50] Samira Patel: We have redaction tools plus explicit allow-list/deny-list policies and schema-level regex restrictions. You can also attach post-filters or run a deterministic verifier as a function call in the pipeline.

[09:10] Samira Patel: Now I'll show function calling that returns structured telemetry and triggers a tool. Demo prompt: "Produce transaction payload and if risk_score > 0.7, call the matcher tool with transaction_id."
[09:23] (Console streaming)
[09:35] Samira Patel: Streaming chunk: {"transaction_id":"tx_7b2","amount_cents":1200,"currency":"USD","merchant_category":"ecommerce","risk_score":0.78,"flags":["fraud_suspected"]} -> runtime triggers tool call: matcher.match({ transaction_id: "tx_7b2" }) -> tool returned: { matched: true, reason: "high velocity from unusual bin" }
[10:02] Maya Lopez: Nice, so the tool output is returned as structured JSON too?
[10:06] Samira Patel: Yup, and you can pipe that into the final response or keep it for internal telemetry. We support nested tool outputs up to a configurable depth, and you can map tool outputs into schema fields.

[11:20] Carlos: Do you have any guardrails around tool invocation frequency? We don't want model to call matcher on every single low-risk txn and blow up our service.
[11:28] Samira Patel: Absolutely - routing policies and rate limits at the request layer. You can set conditional invocation rules (only call matcher when risk_score > 0.7) and Redwood will enforce rate limits and circuit-breakers.

[12:45] Priya Reddy: On the SDK side, can we get typed clients or typescript schemas so devs don't rely on fragile parsing?
[12:52] Jordan Lee: Yes we generate TypeScript types from the schema and provide client helpers that validate responses at runtime. The Console exposes a "download types" button.

[14:10] Carlos: What's the expected latency impact for schema validation + function calls?
[14:16] Samira Patel: Validation itself is negligible (milliseconds). The main cost is the function/tool invocation if it's external - that's typical network latency. For critical low-latency paths we recommend local matcher instances or using the dedicated pool in the same VPC region to keep RTT low. Also Optimize can suggest batching strategies and model variants; e.g., for short payloads a distilled model with quantization keeps tokens low.

[16:00] Samira Patel: Quick aside: our runtime supports prefix/KV caching for repeated user context which is helpful if you enrich similar transactions frequently. That reduces token usage and cost.

[18:20] (demo continues) Samira shows Console policy config: fallback -> try larger model once then fallback to deterministic verifier -> alert on failures.

[20:55] Ethan Shaw: Let's talk compliance; do you retain logs and can we configure retention for audit?
[21:02] Jordan Lee: Yes audit logs are configurable per route. For Private installs you control retention; for Hosted we support enterprise retention tiers and we can push logs to a customer-managed S3. All logs can be encrypted with customer KMS.

[23:10] Carlos: Any SOC2/ISO docs?
[23:14] Avery Chen: Yep, we'll share the SOC2 report and security whitepaper after the call - link in follow-up email.

[24:40] Priya Reddy: For the pilot, what's the minimal dataset you need to run benchmarking?
[24:45] Samira Patel: A few thousand representative transactions is ideal, with labeled outcomes for the success criteria (TP/FP for your risk flag). We can also run synthetic blends. We'll run throughput and latency w/ your worst-case payloads.

[26:00] Carlos: Pricing - ballpark for a pilot and then production?
[26:05] Avery Chen: I'll send a pilot SOW with estimated token budget and a sample pricing sheet; production pricing varies by hosted vs dedicated. For Dedicated there's a monthly commitment for reserved GPU capacity and predictable RPS.

[28:30] Samira Patel: One more demo piece - schema with enums and regex constraints. If user includes merchant phone numbers we redacted them via a post-filter; here's an example: output got rejected because phone didn't match regex so we triggered an inline redaction step.

[30:00] (brief silence while Samira reproduces)
[31:05] Priya Reddy: Are there examples of customers in finance using function calls?
[31:10] Avery Chen: Yes, a few payments customers use function calling to hit deterministic services (fraud matcher, customer ledger) to avoid relying on model memory. We can share anonymized case studies.

[33:20] Maya Lopez: For rollout policy, can we do canary per model variant and route a percentage of traffic?
[33:26] Jordan Lee: Yes you can do canary rollouts, A/B tests, and automatic rollback on quality regression. Console has a traffic split UI and you can tie it to eval sets.

[35:10] Carlos: Ok let's sync practical next steps: pilot, security review, and pricing.
[35:15] Avery Chen: Sounds good. We'll: 1) send pilot SOW and pricing, 2) share SOC2 and security docs, 3) schedule pilot kickoff after we get the dataset.

[36:00] (questions from Ethan about network egress)
[37:12] Jordan Lee: For egress in Hosted we support egress controls and IP allow-lists; but for strict isolation we recommend Private with customer-managed networking.

[39:00] Priya Reddy: One last technical: our models make heavy use of short context windows and we need token-level cost breakdown per route - does Redwood expose that?
[39:08] Samira Patel: Yes Console has token-level breakdown, per-route cost and latency histograms, and trace hooks so you can see per-request kernel choices. Optimize can recommend quantization profiles per model and batching incentives.

[40:30] Carlos: Great, thanks everyone. We'll get the dataset to Priya, and expect the SOW.
[40:40] Avery Chen: Thanks all - we'll follow up with the docs and next steps.
[41:10] (meeting ends)

References/Artifacts shared: demo slide deck (link: https://redwood.example.com/decks/structured-output-demo), security whitepaper (link sent after call), benchmark spreadsheet (link: will share), sample schema attachments in Console.

End of transcript.
